# Phenotypic changes of auditory nerve fibers after excitotoxicity

**Authors:** Artem Diuba; Paul Gratias; Penelope W C Jeffers; Régis Nouvian; Jean-Luc Puel; Sharon G Kujawa; Jérôme Bourien

**Affiliations:** aInstitute for Neuroscience of Montpellier, University of Montpellier, INSERM, Montpellier 34000, France | bEaton-Peabody Laboratories, Massachusetts Eye and Ear, Boston, MA 02114 | cDivision of Medical Sciences, Program in Speech and Hearing Bioscience and Technology, Harvard University, Boston, MA 02115 | dAudiocampus, University of Montpellier, Montpellier 34000, France | eDepartment of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA 02115

## Abstract

This research studied how the cochlea, essential for hearing, recovers from excitotoxic damage. While some connections between nerve cells were permanently lost, the compound action potential of the auditory nerve returned to normal, even exceeding predamage amplitude. This functional retrieval involved changes in the recovered nerve fibers, making them more sensitive. This surprising phenomenon might explain why hearing can recover despite nerve damage, but it could also contribute to overactivity in the brain’s hearing centers, a problem sometimes seen after loud noise exposure.

Keywords: cochlea, excitotoxicity, auditory nerve

## Abstract

There is a substantial body of evidence elucidating the pathophysiological aspects of excitotoxicity in the mammalian cochlea. However, the question of whether the resultant damage is reversible remains unresolved. To replicate an excitotoxic event, we investigated the long-term effects of kainate application in gerbil cochleae. Surprisingly, despite persistent synapse loss, the compound action potential of the auditory nerve fully recovered. This functional retrieval was associated with a phenotypic change in auditory nerve fibers. Thresholds were improved along the tonotopic axis. High-spontaneous rate (SR) fibers largely populated the apical region, while low-SR fibers from the basal region exhibited sound-driven activity indistinguishable from control high-SR fibers. This functional phenotype change may support the full recovery of neural response thresholds and amplitudes after excitotoxicity. Furthermore, hyperresponsiveness of the auditory nerve fibers could be a crucial factor in the development of hyperactivity in the central auditory pathways, a common occurrence following acoustic overstimulation.

The excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate mediates synaptic communication between sensory inner hair cells (IHCs) and the type I auditory nerve fibers (ANFs) that carry the afferent outflow (95%) from the cochlea to the brainstem (1). The release of glutamate from IHCs onto afferent terminals operates at the synaptic contact, populated by a presynaptic organelle, known as the ribbon body. In rodents, most of the ANF terminals form a single synaptic contact with a single IHC, whereas each IHC forms synapses with multiple (~12 to 20) ANFs (2). A minority of ANFs (5%), the type II fibers, form ribbon synapses with outer hair cells (OHCs), and each type II fiber synapses with multiple OHCs via en passant connections after turning toward the base of the cochlea (3). While both type I and type II fibers are excited by glutamate (3, 4), it has also been shown that type II afferents can respond to adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to signal OHC destruction (5, 6).

When excessively released from the IHC (1) or incompletely recycled (7–9), glutamate has neurotoxic properties, a phenomenon called excitotoxicity. Previous reports have shown that both high-level sound (10–12) and glutamate agonists such as α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) or kainate (kainic acid, KA) can cause the type I but not type II terminals to swell and become damaged (13). These detrimental effects can be blocked by glutamate antagonists (1, 14, 15). In addition, evidence suggests that glutamate overexposure at the ribbon synapse leads to toxic levels of cytosolic calcium within the type I afferent terminal due to the activity of calcium-permeable AMPA receptors at the synapse (16, 17). As in other parts of the nervous system, the resulting neural damage is characterized by a two-step mechanism: i) a massive ion and water entry leading to an acute swelling, which results in disruption of postsynaptic structures (i.e., type I afferent terminals contacting IHCs), and ii) a neuronal death (i.e., type I spiral ganglion neurons) triggered by Ca2+ entry, a cascade of metabolic events, including free-radical production, protease, and endonuclease activation [see among others: (18–20)].

A considerable body of evidence exists describing excitotoxic consequences of cochlear-applied glutamate agonists. Direct injection of the glutamate agonist KA into the cochlea resulted in acute swelling of afferent terminals below the IHCs and 34% loss of type I spiral ganglion neurons 10 d later in rats (21) and up to 60% loss in Budgerigar within 2 or more months following injury (22). As a consequence, compound action potentials (CAPs) of the auditory nerve and auditory brainstem response (ABR) wave I amplitudes were permanently reduced. However, in guinea pigs, 10-min intracochlear perfusion of agonist AMPA induced acute swelling of afferent terminals that recovered within 5 d, along with restoration of CAP thresholds and amplitudes (1). Similar results were observed following high-concentration KA application onto the round window membrane of the chinchilla cochlea (23). Despite the initial swelling and disruption of afferent terminals, CAP thresholds returned to normal within 5 d, with CAP amplitudes recovering over a longer period of 30 d. Histological examination revealed a qualitatively normal pattern of IHC innervation 10 d after KA treatment. A study in chickens further elucidated the dose-dependent nature of KA-induced excitotoxicity reversal (24). Depending on the concentration of KA injected into the basilar papilla, peripheral axons demonstrated the ability to extend new neurites, facilitating synaptogenesis to reestablish synaptic connections with IHC targets.

Beyond the overall findings of substantial recovery following excitotoxic insult, the relationship between structural and functional recovery has never been quantitatively resolved. Neural response thresholds are quite insensitive to even dramatic IHC, synaptic and afferent neural loss (25–28), and neural response amplitudes do not reflect activity of all ANFs (29). Thus, apparent recovery of function may mask persistent underlying injury. In addition, the ANF subtypes categorized according to their spontaneous firing rate of discharge [SR (30)] differ in their threshold and sound-driven activity and appear to be differentially vulnerable to insult (29, 31, 32). Moreover, it is not known whether ANFs keep such original characteristics after excitotoxic insult.

Here, we investigated acute and long-term effects of KA application into the round-window niche on various electrophysiological indices, including auditory nerve single-unit and compound neural responses. Distortion product otoacoustic emissions (DPOAEs) excluded KA effects on OHCs. We correlated electrophysiological data with the temporal dynamics of IHC ribbon synapse degeneration and subsequent repair. Despite the persistence of substantial synapse loss throughout the cochlea, CAP fully recovered following KA-induced excitotoxicity. This functional recovery was accompanied by a phenotypic shift in single units of the auditory nerve, rendering them significantly more responsive to sound. An unfortunate consequence of this increased activity, however, is a possible instigating role in pathophysiological processes leading to hyperacusis and tinnitus after excitotoxic events with high relevance to human hearing, such as sound overexposure, including a lifetime of accumulated exposures of the aging ear.

## Materials and Methods

Detailed Materials and Methods are available in SI Appendix.

### Animals.

Young adult Mongolian gerbils (3 to 4 mo, female) were obtained from Charles River Laboratories (L’Arbresle, France). The animals were housed in facilities accredited by the French Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry (Ministère de l’Agriculture et de la Forêt, Agreement C-34-172-36), and the experimental protocol was approved (Authorization CEEA-LR-12111) by the Animal Ethics Committee of Languedoc-Roussillon (France). The experiments were carried out in accordance with the animal welfare guidelines 2010/63/EC of the European Communities Council Directive regarding the care and use of animals for experimental procedures. All efforts were made to minimize the number and suffering of the animals used.

### Drug Preparation and Application.

Artificial perilymph (AP) served as the control solution and vehicle for KA. It consisted of the following (in mM): 137 NaCl, 5 KCl, 2 CaCl2, 1 MgCl2, 1 NaHCO3, and 11 glucose; pH 7.4, osmolarity 304 ± 4.3 mosmol/L. Before each experiment, KA (Sigma, St. Louis, MO) was prepared in AP to a final concentration of 25 mM. Control and KA solutions were applied into the round window niche for 60 min (SI Appendix).

### Physiological Assessments.

Physiological assessments were performed on anesthetized animals in sound-proof chambers, with body temperature maintained at 38 ± 1 °C.

#### CAP recording.

Acoustic stimuli (10-ms duration, 1-ms rise/fall time) were presented by varying intensities from 0 to 80 dB SPL in 5-dB steps (200 presentations/level, random order) at a rate of 11/s with alternating polarity. CAPs were recorded from an electrode placed on the edge of the round window niche. Electrical signal was amplified (5,000×) and filtered (300 to 3,000 Hz). Amplitude measurements were done between the first negative wave (N1) and the baseline. CAP threshold was defined as the sound level needed to elicit a measurable response (>1 μV).

#### Single-unit recordings of the auditory nerve.

Animals were prepared for single-unit recordings from the auditory nerve, as previously described (33). Fiber spontaneous rate of discharge (SR) was evaluated by averaging the firing (spikes/s) over 30 s. Characteristic frequency (CF) of the fiber was determined using a threshold-tracking program (10 spikes/s > SR). The rate-intensity (RI) function of each fiber was recorded using tone bursts presented at the fiber’s CF (trapezoid envelope, 1-ms rise/fall time, 50-ms duration, 10 bursts/s). Firing rate was estimated as the average rate for the overall duration of the tone burst for a range of stimulus levels varying from 0 to 80 dB SPL in 4 dB steps (60 presentations per level, random level order). A peristimulus-time histogram (PSTH) of each fiber was recorded in response to 60 dB SPL tone bursts presented at CF (trapezoid envelope, 1-ms rise/fall time, 50-ms duration, 10 bursts/s, 180 presentations).

### Morphological Assessments.

#### Light microscopy.

After the electrophysiological session, the animals were decapitated under deep anesthesia, and their cochleae were fixed with a solution of 2.5% glutaraldehyde (1×, pH 7.4) The cochleae were then embedded in EmBed 812. Thin sections (70 nm) were collected at different levels of cochlea and observed with NanoZoomer S20 (Hamamatsu).

#### Confocal imaging.

Quantification of the number of the synaptic ribbons has been described elsewhere (29). Briefly, the cochleas were perfused with 4% paraformaldehyde in 1× PBS, pH 7.3, and postfixed for 30 min in the same fixative at room temperature. The presynaptic IHC ribbons were labeled using a mouse anti-CtBP2 IgG1 antibody (at a dilution of 1:500, BD Biosciences, San Diego, CA). Glutamate receptors were identified using a mouse monoclonal antibody raised against the C-terminus of the GluA2 subunits IgG2a [clone 6C4, 1:200 dilution Millipore, Billerica, MA; (34)]. The secondary antibodies were an Alexa 488 labeled goat anti-IgG1 mouse antibody together with an Alexa 568 labeled goat anti-IgG2 mouse antibody (1:1,000, Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA). CtBP2/GluA2 receptor colocalization, defining a ribbon-anchored synapse, was determined in each z-plane by intersected ribbon and AMPA receptor labeling delimitation. Detailed procedures for determining the number of synapses, measuring ribbon volume, and locating ribbons along the modiolar–pillar axis are provided in SI Appendix.

### Statistics.

Data are expressed as mean ± SEM. Normality of the variables was tested by the Shapiro–Wilk test. To compare two samples, a Student’s t test was used if conditions for a parametric test were met. Otherwise, the comparison was evaluated by a Wilcoxon rank-sum test.

In the case of 3 or more samples, if conditions for a parametric test were met, the significance of the group differences was assessed with an ANOVA test. Once the significance of the group differences (P < 0.05) was established, Tukey’s post hoc tests were subsequently used for pairwise comparisons. If conditions were not met, Kruskal–Wallis tests were used. If the group differences were significant (P < 0.05), Dunn’s tests were then used for post hoc comparisons between pairs of groups.

## Results

This study was performed to investigate a long-term effect of KA-induced cochlear excitotoxicity. Several questions were addressed. First, does KA reach the upper region of the cochlea when applied on the round window niche? Second, how long does it take for the auditory nerve to degenerate and regenerate/repair from excitotoxicity? Third, do the discharge patterns of the repaired ANFs change?

### Acute Effect of Round Window Kainate Application.

In a first set of experiments, the CAP amplitude of the auditory nerve was monitored during a 60-min application of control AP alone or AP containing 25 mM KA, as well as for 30 min after application (Fig. 1A). The CAP reflects the synchronous firing of a population of ANFs in response to a sound stimulus. Analysis of CAP amplitudes evoked by tone bursts at 60 dB SPL revealed distinct time course characteristics depending on the subpopulation of fibers activated along the tonotopic axis (35). Specifically, the CAP evoked by a 16 kHz tone burst (ANFs located at 25% from the base) rapidly diminished and completely disappeared within the first 20 min following the onset of KA application (Fig. 1A). An exponential fit of the CAP data allowed for the estimation of a decay time constant (τ), corresponding to a 63% decrease in amplitude. For the 16 kHz CAP, the τ value equals 4.7 min, indicating that the CAP decreased by 95% within 14.1 min (Fig. 1B). In contrast, the CAP amplitude evoked by a 2 kHz tone burst (ANFs located at 35% from the apex) exhibited a slower decrease, reaching a 63% reduction after 1 h of KA application (τ = 59.3 min), and completely disappeared 30 min after cessation of KA application. These findings suggest that when KA is applied to the round window niche, it initially affects ANFs innervating the base of the cochlea before affecting those in the mid-apex region. At the end of the electrophysiological recordings, the cochlea was removed and prepared for morphological analysis. Consistent with the total abolishment of the CAPs, we observed a massive swelling and disruption of afferent synapses below IHCs in both the apical (2 kHz) and basal (16 kHz) regions of the cochlea (Fig. 1C).

### Long-Term Effects of Acute Kainate Application.

#### DPOAEs and CAPs of the auditory nerve.

In a second set of experiments, DPOAEs and CAPs of the auditory nerve were monitored at various time points after the KA application. To account for potential age-related variations, all data were normalized to the AP-control group of the same age.

DPOAEs did not exhibit significant changes at any of the recorded time points compared to the AP control (SI Appendix, Fig. S1), indicating that KA did not adversely affect the function of OHCs, as already shown in chinchilla (36). Conversely, the CAP of the auditory nerve gradually reappeared over the course of days and weeks following KA application (Fig. 2 A–D). However, the time taken for the CAP threshold to return to its initial value varied depending on the frequency of stimulation, with τ values ranging from 1.5 to 4.8 d (Fig. 2E). Although the CAP amplitude displayed a similar base-to-apex gradient of recovery, it required significantly longer time to reach control values (Fig. 2 F–H). Three hours after application, the CAP amplitudes remained tremendously reduced compared to initial values. Over time, a slow and gradual recovery was observed with the recovery period ranging from approximately 3 to 20 wk. However, the time course was frequency- and intensity-dependent. Notably, the 16 kHz-CAP amplitude at 40 dB SPL recovered much earlier (τ = 16.0 d) compared to the CAP recovery at 2 kHz (τ = 99.8 d, Fig. 2H).

#### Synapse count.

Next, we estimated the number of ribbon-anchored synapses along the tonotopic axis by assessing the juxtaposition of the presynaptic ribbon organelle of IHCs and the postsynaptic density using immunohistochemistry (Fig. 3A). In AP control cochleae processed at 1, 14, 28, or 135 d, we observed a bimodal distribution of synapses per IHC, with prominent maxima in the 2 and 16 kHz cochlear regions (Fig. 3B), as already shown in nontreated cochleae (37). In contrast, 1 d after KA application, a drastic reduction in the number of synapses of approximately 80% was observed (Fig. 3C). Worthy of note was the presence of orphan ribbons at day 1 all along the tonotopic axis of the cochlea, especially in the 4, 8, and 16 kHz regions. Synaptic repair continued up to 20 wk, reaching 59, 60, 54, and 65% of recovery in the 16, 8, 4, and 2 kHz cochlear regions, respectively. These results therefore confront us with a paradoxical phenomenon: a complete recovery of the CAP despite 40% fewer ribbon synapses.

#### Single-fiber recordings from the auditory nerve.

To address this apparent contradiction, we recorded single-unit responses of the auditory nerve 20 wk after KA application, by which time the CAP was fully recovered regardless of the frequency and intensity tested.

#### Threshold and spontaneous discharge rate.

In KA-treated animals, we found improved thresholds across the entire ANF population (Fig. 4 A–C). To probe whether the change in threshold was frequency-dependent (35, 38–41), we split the ANF population into 2 groups of approximately equal size according to the distribution of the CF along the tonotopic axis (CF ≤ 3.6 kHz and CF > 3.6 kHz). Both low- and high-CF fibers showed lower thresholds following excitotoxicity (Fig. 4C). While the enhanced sensitivity at lower CFs coincided with a significant increase in SR of discharge, the change in threshold of high-CF fibers was not associated with an increase in SR (Fig. 4 D–F). We then examined the distribution of fibers according to SR (30). In control animals, the SR histogram exhibited the classical bimodal shape (Fig. 4G). In KA-treated cochleae, the proportion of low-SR fibers (SR ≤ 18 spikes/s) was reduced from 29 to 23%, whereas the number of high-SR fibers (SR > 18 spikes/s) increased (Fig. 4H). When compared to controls, the parallel shift of the cumulative distribution of KA-treated ANFs toward the right confirms that ANFs that recovered from excitotoxicity had significantly increased SRs (Fig. 4I). A further analysis of the fibers’ distribution according to CF did not show a significant difference between control and KA-treated cochleae (Fig. 4 J–L). This confirms that the changes in threshold and SR in KA-treated cochleae cannot be attributed to a sampling issue due to single-fiber recording technique in gerbils (35, 38, 40, 42).

#### Rate intensity function.

The shape of rate-intensity function reflects, in part, the nonlinear basilar membrane input/output function, modulated by the outer hair cell-driven gain-control mechanism and the synaptic properties between inner hair cells and ANFs (reviewed in refs. 43 and 44). To preserve our preparation, we limited tone levels to 80 dB SPL, impeding a large fraction of ANFs from reaching saturation state. Thus, best fit of the rate-intensity function was obtained using Yates’ fitting model [(45), SI Appendix, Fig. S2]. Using derivative function of the fit, we approximated the sound level at maximum slope (Fig. 5 A–D). In control animals, sound level at maximum slope of each ANF showed a negative correlation with the SR in both low- and high-frequency coding regions (Fig. 5 E and G). In contrast, this correlation was abolished in KA-treated animals, suggesting a violation of the canonical threshold–SR relationship after excitotoxic injury (Fig. 5 F and H). According to previous studies (39, 41), we found a negative correlation between the maximum slope and SR only in the low-CF fibers. However, the maximum slope and SR relationship significantly increased in KA-treated animals for both low- (Fig. 5 I and J) and high-CF fibers (Fig. 5 K and L). In the framework of a synaptic control of the maximum slope in the rate-intensity functions (39, 41), this analysis argues for a greater synaptic contribution to the shaping of rate-intensity functions following excitotoxicity.

#### Peristimulus time histograms (PSTHs).

The shape of the rate-intensity functions also differed as a function of CF and SR in KA-treated animals. In the low-CF fibers, discharge rate tended to increase in KA-treated animals, especially at low levels of stimulation, i.e., up to 60 dB SPL (Fig. 6 A and B). In the high-CF fibers, the discharge rate increased in KA-treated animals for low-SR fibers across all levels of stimulation (Fig. 6C). In contrast, the high SRs of the high-frequency coding region were not affected by KA treatment (Fig. 6D).

Using PSTHs, we then resolved the effect of KA on ANFs based on their respective CF and SR (30). At the supraliminal intensity level which engages the vast majority of ANFs (60 dB SPL, Fig. 4 A and B), PSTHs in the low-frequency coding region were almost comparable between control and KA-treated animals (Fig. 6 E and F). In control animals, PSTH peak and plateau were significantly larger in high-SR fibers in comparison to low-SR fibers (peak: 537 ± 42.6 spikes/s vs. 674 ± 20.1 spikes/s from low- and high-SR fibers, respectively; plateau: 139 ± 10.4 spikes/s vs. 164 ± 4.9 spikes/s from low- and high-SR fibers, respectively; Fig. 6 I and J). In contrast, we did not observe such significant differences in KA-treated animals, as the low-SR fibers tended to increase their discharge rate (peak: 620 ± 79.9 spikes/s vs. 693 ± 17.8 spikes/s from low- and high-SR fibers, respectively; plateau: 170 ± 17 spikes/s vs. 167 ± 3.5 spikes/s from low- and high-SR fibers, respectively; Fig. 6 I and J). In the same manner, PSTH peak latency was significantly shorter in high-SR fibers in comparison to low-SR fibers in control animals (latency: 4.2 ± 0.21 ms vs. 3.5 ± 0.11 ms from low- and high-SR fibers, respectively). Here again, no significant difference in the PSTH peak latency was observed in KA-treated animals (latency: 4.1 ± 0.4 ms vs. 3.3 ± 0.1 ms from low- and high-SR fibers, respectively; Fig. 6K).

At high-frequency coding regions, PSTH peak and plateau dramatically increased after KA for low-SR fibers (peak: 553 ± 45.8 spikes/s vs. 741 ± 33.1 spikes/s from control and KA-treated, respectively; plateau: 160 ± 11.5 spikes/s vs. 206 ± 8.6 spikes/s from control and KA-treated, respectively; Fig. 6 G, L, and M). High-SR fiber PSTHs were not affected after KA-treatment (peak: 823 ± 12.8 spikes/s vs. 831 ± 17.9 spikes/s from control and KA-treated, respectively; plateau: 204 ± 3.7 spikes/s vs. 209 ± 4.1 spikes/s from control and KA-treated, respectively; Fig. 6 H, L, and M). PSTH peak latency decreased in control animals with increasing SR (3.3 ± 0.22 ms vs. 2.2 ± 0.04 ms in control low SR and high SR, respectively, Fig. 6N). In contrast, no difference was found in the PSTH peak latency after KA treatment, regardless of SR (2.4 ± 0.13 ms vs. 2.3 ± 0.06 ms in low and high SR, respectively, Fig. 6N). Notably, the low-SR fibers in KA-treated animals displayed PSTH peak latencies over a similar range as that of high-SR fibers from the control group (2.4 ± 0.13 ms in low-SR KA-treated animals vs. 2.2 ± 0.04 ms in high-SR control animals; Fig. 6N).

#### Morphological changes of the ribbon synapse.

Next, we investigated whether this functional phenotypic ANF change correlates with ultrastructural changes at the synapse machinery level (46–49). Here, we returned to confocal data to correlate the volume of the synaptic ribbon with its location along the modiolar–pillar axis of the IHC (Fig. 7 A–H). As reported in untreated gerbils (50), the AP-treated cochleae exhibited larger normalized ribbon volume on the modiolar side (1.052 ± 0.016) than on the pillar side (0.969 ± 0.012, Fig. 7D). Sixty-three percent of ribbons were located on the pillar side, and 37% on the modiolar side (Inset, Fig. 7C). In KA-treated animals, normalized volume difference between modiolar and pillar ribbons was not significant (modiolus, 1.008 ± 0.025; pillar, 0.993 ± 0.021; Fig. 7H), with a more balanced modiolar/pillar distribution of ribbon synapses (45 vs. 55% for the modiolar and the pillar locations, respectively, Inset Fig. 7G). Cumulative distribution of ribbon volume showed a broader distribution in KA-treated cochleae (0.63 to 1.48, 10 to 90% interval) compared to control (0.68 to 1.35, 10 to 90% interval, Fig. 7I), reflecting greater heterogeneity of ribbon volume in KA animals. Conversely, KA-treated animals showed a narrower distribution of ribbons around the modiolar–pillar axis (−1.7 to 2 µm, 10 to 90% interval) than in AP control (−1.77 to 2.83 µm, 10 to 90% interval; Fig. 7J).

Taken together, these data highlight significant changes in low-SR ANF physiology and IHC-ribbon morphology in repaired synapses following KA-induced excitotoxicity. Particularly striking are low-SR/low-threshold fibers, with sound-driven activities akin to high-SR fibers. Consequently, this phenotypic shift may compensate for KA-induced fiber loss, enabling the recovery of CAP amplitudes despite a 40% reduction in ribbon synapses.

## Discussion

Our study reveals a remarkable phenotypic shift in ANFs following KA-induced excitotoxicity, rendering them significantly more responsive to sound. With the exception of the high-SR fibers from the basal region, most ANFs underwent a phenotype change. While thresholds of ANFs were improved along the tonotopic axis, SR increased only at the apical part of the cochlea and not at the basal region. At the apical region, a large fraction of high-SR fibers was found after KA treatment, accounting for the SR increase. At the basal region of the cochlea, where the SR did not change, low-SR fibers exhibited sound-driven activity akin to control high-SR fibers. This phenotypic shift may explain the seemingly paradoxical observation of complete recovery of CAP amplitudes despite a substantial and enduring loss of synapses. A critical question arising from these findings is whether these phenotypic changes are specific to the KA-induced excitotoxicity model or whether they represent a more general phenomenon observed in other forms of excitotoxic injury, such as those associated with noise trauma or neurodegenerative diseases.

### Differences between Excitotoxic Models, Species, or Strain.

Cochlear synaptopathy can be induced by various excitotoxic challenges, including injection of glutamate agonists into the cochlea (1, 21, 36), acoustic overexposure (51, 52), ischemia (13), and ototoxic drugs (53), as well as the losses that occur during aging without and with noise exposure (54–56). All of these models have been used to study cochlear synaptopathic consequences of excitotoxicity. The extent of synaptic injury, as well as the degree of recovery in the case of the exposure models, are shaped by characteristics of the individual (e.g., species, strain, age, sex) and characteristics of the exposure (type and dose of the drug or noise) as well as when the outcomes are quantified in postexposure time as addressed below.

#### Comparison between pharmacological and ecological models of excitotoxicity.

Application of ouabain, a Na+/K+-ATPase inhibitor, into the round window niche of the gerbil cochlea significantly reduced the number of IHC ribbons (29, 57), and later, caused loss of the cell bodies of affected neurons (58–60), leading to an irreversible and dose-dependent increase in CAP threshold and decrease in CAP amplitude. In contrast, the CAP of the auditory nerve recovered in guinea pig and chinchilla cochleae after application of glutamate agonists AMPA and KA, respectively (1, 23). Ultrastructural examination of these cochleae revealed that CAP recovery was linked to spontaneous regrowth of afferent terminals, a reconnection with IHCs, and synaptogenesis (14, 61). In chickens, the reversibility of the functional loss was found to be dependent on dose; however, no histopathology was studied (24). While functional evaluations were well documented, the functionally important structural changes remain to be clarified.

Studies of noise-induced synaptopathy are more abundant and provide quantitative data, including over longer periods. Although acoustic overstimulation typically affects OHCs, leading to elevated cochlear thresholds and permanent hearing loss, hair cells are not the most vulnerable elements to acoustic overexposure (51, 62). Noise exposures that result in only transient threshold shifts and no hair cell death can nevertheless produce dramatic loss of ribbon synapses, beginning at noise doses well below those that result in permanent threshold elevations and persistent hair cell injury (28). Noise-induced synaptopathy can be prevented by IEM-1460, a selective blocker of GluA2-lacking AMPA receptors, suggesting that acute swelling and disruption of afferent terminals are mediated by Ca2+-permeable AMPA receptors (16, 17).

Since the pioneering work of Schuknecht (63, 64), age-related hearing losses have been classified according to different patterns of cell type degeneration, i.e., hair cells, neurons, and strial cells (65, 66). Although essentially all humans and animals lose cochlear afferent synapses with age (67, 68), only a subset of cases qualify for a label of neural presbycusis, defined as a significant loss of ANF peripheral axons with minimal degeneration of hair cells. Low-SR neurons appear to be preferentially vulnerable to aging (31, 41, 54, 69–75). Thus, exaggerating the effects of aging per se, deafferentation of the IHCs and subsequent neural degeneration in the aging cochlea might also be triggered by the accumulation of excitotoxic noise insults over the lifespan (51, 55).

#### Species or strain differences.

In addition to differences in the experimental approach (pharmacological vs. noise and age), discrepancies may arise from variations in species or strain. In adult CBA/CaJ mice, noise-induced synaptopathy occurs rapidly and is persistent to 2 y or more (51, 55, 62). Conversely, in guinea pigs, counts of immunostained synaptic puncta correlate with increasing postexposure survival (72, 76). Furthermore, different capacities for spontaneous synaptic repair have been reported. While CBA/CaJ mice show small, acute recoveries, with quantification complicated by transient downregulation of surface AMPA receptor expression and immunostaining intensity (77–79), they can also show dramatic postnoise losses that persist 2 y later (51, 55). In contrast, studies in C57Bl/6 mice have demonstrated significant synapse recovery/repair in the most affected region (80, 81). A permanent reduction of ABR wave 1/CAP amplitude after noise exposure has been highly correlated with persistent loss of synapses (28), whereas mice receiving nonsynaptopathic exposures show full ABR wave 1/CAP amplitude recovery (28, 55, 80, 82, 83). Paradoxically, normal return of CAP amplitude despite permanent synapse loss has been reported in noise-exposed gerbils (52). This phenomenon likely relies on the different proportion of low-, medium-, and high-SR fibers across species [low, SR≤0.5 spike/s; medium, 0.5 < SR ≤ 18 spikes/s; high, SR >18 spikes/s; according to Liberman (30)]. In mice, low-SR fibers represent only approximately 10% of the full contingent of fibers (84). Consequently, a 50% loss of synapses induced by a noise exposure (51) depletes the low-SR fibers as well as a significant number of medium- and/or high-SR fibers, resulting in reduced CAP amplitudes. The fact that gerbils exhibit a larger proportion of low-SR fibers in the basal part of the cochlea (~30%), which poorly contribute to the CAP amplitude (29), may explain the return to normal amplitude of the CAP, despite substantial permanent ribbon synapse loss.

### Single-Unit Recordings from the Gerbil Auditory Nerve.

To deepen our understanding of this conundrum, we conducted single-unit recordings from the auditory nerve 20 wk after KA administration, a timeframe aligned with the return of CAP amplitudes to control values. Remarkably, ANF thresholds appeared not only normal but slightly decreased compared to pre-excitotoxic levels, consistent with increased SR.

#### Species differences.

Few studies have investigated the impact of synaptopathy on sound coding using single-unit recording. Although Furman et al. (32) described a notable reduction in the population of low-SR fibers in the basal half portion of the guinea pig cochlea 2 wk after noise exposure, no change in the basic properties was seen in the remaining fibers. In our study, we divided the ANF population into two categories: low-SR (SR ≤ 18 spikes/s) and high-SR (SR > 18 spikes/s) fibers. In KA-treated animals, high-SR fibers largely populated the apical region, while low-SR fibers from the basal region exhibited sound-driven activity indistinguishable from control high-spontaneous fibers. Analysis of PSTHs confirmed these phenotypic changes in low-SR fibers, with enhancements in both onset and steady-state responses—onset latencies close to those of high-SR fibers and increased onset synchrony of firing (less low-SR “jitter” is reflected in the more robust CAP amplitudes after KA). Albeit using a 5 ms tone pip, Suthakar and Liberman (85) reported similar results in CBA/CaJ mice 2 wk after noise exposure. They demonstrated increased peak and steady-state firing rates, reduced jitter in first-spike latencies, and improved resistance to noise. In contrast to our results, Suthakar and Liberman’s study showed no significant differences in SR histograms for normal vs. exposed ears. There was no significant increase in SR or improvement in threshold and no evidence of dynamic range alterations.

#### Amount and the location of synapse loss.

One straightforward explanation for the discrepancies between our study and others is the difference in the time points at which single-unit recordings were conducted [10 d for Zheng et al. (23), 2 wk for Furman et al. (32), and Suthakar and Liberman (85) vs. 20 wk in the present study], as well as the species used (chinchilla, guinea pig, mouse, and gerbil). However, the amount and location of synapse loss also may contribute to observed differences. In our KA-treated gerbil cochleae, we found 40% synapse loss all along the tonotopic axis. In noise-exposed guinea pigs (32), the synapse reduction is shaped by the frequency content of the noise exposure band, and for the band used in that study, injury increased toward the base, with a maximum loss close to 30% at 32 kHz. However, the synaptic changes were not those predicted from simply eliminating the low-SR elements [i.e., large ribbons on the modiolar side (86)]. Rather, there was an increase in mean ribbon size, with no obvious decrease in the proportion of synapses originating on the modiolar side compared with the pillar side. In agreement with our data, the relationship between ribbon size and SR was not correlated, since a decrease in the ribbon size of IHC-ANF synapses from the modiolar side was observed, despite no change in SR 1 d following noise exposure (86). Here, we found no significant volume change in IHC ribbons located on the modiolar side 20 wk after KA exposure, while low-SR ANFs exhibited thresholds and sound-driven activity comparable to those of high-SR fibers. The increased number of high-SR/low-threshold fibers, coupled with enhanced onset and steady-state responses of the low-SR fibers, accounts for the full recovery of CAP amplitudes despite a substantial loss of synapses. This homeostatic plasticity might stem from a change in the neurotransmitter release properties (87, 88) and/or from different intrinsic excitability of the ANFs due to the postsynaptic receptor change (89) or branching in the recovered ANFs (1). Alternatively, lateral efferents that contact postsynaptic terminals that have been recovered/repaired might also contribute to the adaptative mechanism compensating for synapse loss after excitotoxicity (61).

Many cochlear pathologies involve excitotoxic events. The discovery that recovered ANFs can exhibit phenotypic shifts to compensate for synapse loss following excitotoxicity is significant. This plasticity at the first synapse may also be a crucial contributor to the development of hyperactivity within central auditory pathways, a phenomenon frequently observed after acoustic overstimulation (90). This, in turn, may be one source of tinnitus or hyperacusis, abnormal auditory perceptions commonly associated with acoustic overexposure (91). Recent work has shown that mice exposed to excitotoxic noise with or without permanent threshold sensitivity losses show behavioral evidence of loudness hyperacusis (92, 93), and human studies have revealed reductions in suprathreshold ABR wave 1 amplitude in tinnitus vs. non-tinnitus subjects with normal thresholds (94–96). Overall, this discovery underscores a remarkable mechanism for self-repair within the cochlea and paves the way for future research aimed at developing therapies for cochlear pathologies.
